rejected.title: Worldviews and support for sustainability
card: A worldview is the set of values and beliefs a person uses to judge what matters. People with different worldviews can look at the same environment and see different things.
Worldviews shape which actions people support. Someone who values a forest mainly for timber and jobs may back logging it. Someone who values it for its own sake may back protecting it.
So groups can disagree about the same plan, such as limiting development near a forest. They may agree on the facts and still disagree about what matters most.
Each side weighs the costs and benefits, such as jobs or habitat, in a different way. Knowing the worldviews behind a dispute helps explain why it happens.
rejected.remember: Worldviews shape which actions people support, so groups can disagree over the same plan.

a.q: Two groups read the same report on a forest. One wants it logged and the other wants it protected. What best explains their disagreement?
opts: They hold different worldviews about what matters
One group misunderstood the facts in the report
One group values the forest and the other does not
The report favoured one group over the other
a.why: Worldviews shape what people value, so groups can read the same facts and still want different actions. The tempting option is that one group got the facts wrong, but groups may agree on the facts and still disagree. Both groups value the forest, one for timber and jobs and the other for its own sake.
a.clue: They can agree on the facts and still differ on what matters.

b.q: A council in Gippsland plans to limit new housing beside a wetland. Sam and Jo both accept the housing would shrink the wetland. Sam backs the plan because the wetland matters for its own sake. Jo opposes it because the housing would bring jobs. What best explains why they disagree?
opts: They weigh the wetland and the jobs differently
They disagree on whether the wetland would shrink
They have each read a different housing plan
Sam knows more facts about the wetland than Jo
b.why: Sam and Jo agree on what the housing would do, so the facts are not the issue. Sam values the wetland for its own sake and Jo puts jobs first, so their worldviews lead them to different views of the same plan.
b.clue: Check what Sam and Jo already agree on.

flags: Question a, wording: Two wrong options use absolutes ('Only one group cares', 'must have contained wrong facts') where the card says groups 'can' disagree and 'may' agree on facts. A test-wise student can rule them out without knowing the idea.
Question b, wording: The wrong option 'Jo holds no worldview about the wetland at all' uses an absolute that makes it easy to rule out without knowing the idea.

draft.title: Worldviews and support for sustainability
card: A worldview is the set of values and beliefs a person uses to judge what matters. People with different worldviews can look at the same environment and see different things.
Human-centred
a worldview that values nature mainly for what it gives people, such as timber, jobs or farmland. People who hold it may back actions that protect nature when the protection helps people.
Earth-centred
a worldview that sees nature as worth protecting for its own sake. People who hold it may back actions such as protecting a forest even when it costs people something.
This is why groups can disagree about the same plan, such as limiting development near a forest. They may agree on the facts and still disagree about what matters most.
draft.remember: Worldviews shape which actions people support, so groups can disagree over the same plan.

a.q: Two groups read the same report on a forest. One wants it logged and the other wants it protected. What best explains their disagreement?
opts: They hold different worldviews about what matters
One group has not been able to read the report
Only one group cares about the environment at all
The report must have contained wrong facts
a.why: Worldviews shape what people value, so groups can read the same facts and still want different actions. The tempting option is that the facts are wrong, but the card says groups may agree on the facts and still disagree.
a.clue: They can agree on the facts and still differ on what matters.

b.q: A council in Gippsland plans to limit new housing beside a wetland. Sam supports it because the wetland has a right to exist, even though the housing would bring jobs. Which worldview does Sam's support show?
opts: Earth-centred, as it values nature for its own sake
Human-centred, as it values nature for the jobs it brings
Human-centred, as it values nature for its own sake
Earth-centred, as it values nature for the jobs it brings
b.why: Sam backs protection even though it costs jobs, and gives the wetland's own right to exist as the reason. That is an earth-centred worldview. A human-centred view would value the wetland mainly for what it gives people.
b.clue: Look at the reason Sam gives, not just the action.

a.best: They hold different worldviews about what matters

b.best: Earth-centred, as it values nature for its own sake

final.title: Worldviews and support for sustainability
card: A worldview is the set of values and beliefs a person uses to judge what matters. People with different worldviews can look at the same environment and see different things.
Worldviews shape which actions people support. Someone who values a forest mainly for timber and jobs may back logging it. Someone who values it for its own sake may back protecting it.
So groups can disagree about the same plan, such as limiting development near a forest. They may agree on the facts and still disagree about what matters most.
Each side weighs the costs and benefits, such as jobs or habitat, in a different way. Knowing the worldviews behind a dispute helps explain why it happens.
